title: Oracy floats on a sea of knowledge
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau responds to the UK Education Secretary's announcement that oracy will become a new strand of the English curriculum with equal status to reading and writing. He grants the case for it: formal speech must be taught, talk is a cognitive lever, and oracy has long been a marker of privilege. His objection is that the best way to help children speak well is to ensure they know a great deal about what they are speaking about, which he illustrates with a failed school public speaking team and the classic baseball study on reading comprehension. He then examines the evidence base, finding that the EEF's six months' progress figure mostly reflects reading outcomes, that Neil Mercer's Thinking Together findings are modest, and that large evaluations of oracy programmes show little effect. He also warns that assessing oracy risks measuring personality and middle-class speech, and he recommends rhetoric teaching inside a knowledge-rich curriculum instead.
points: Didau agrees that formal speech, unlike everyday conversation, must be explicitly taught, and that making students answer audibly and at length is simply good teaching.
His core claim is that talk leverages what children know, so a knowledge-rich curriculum does more for speaking than separate lessons on speaking skills.

He argues the headline evidence is weaker than it looks, since oral language interventions mostly measure reading gains and a large evaluation of about 400 primary schools found an effect size of 0.02.
Oracy assessment was removed from the GCSE because it could not be marked consistently, and he fears it would now reward extroversion and middle-class speech.
He splits the Commission's three strands and finds that learning to talk is mostly unteachable, learning through talk is just good teaching, and only learning about talk is real curriculum knowledge.
quotes: Talk leverages what children know; if they don’t know enough, they won’t have much to say. You can only speak eloquently about things you know well.
Formal speech has to be taught. Everyday conversation — an example of what David Geary calls biologically primary knowledge — is picked up though exposure.

Insisting that students answer audibly and at length, that they use academic vocabulary and respond to their peers’ contributions is just good teaching. If the oracy movement gets more teachers doing this then it will have done some good.
Being clever and being knowledgeable may not be the same thing, but, as was clear to me and my students, knowledge trumped all else.

Talking, like collaborating, solving problems and being creative, is something human beings have been doing for tens of thousands of years. These so-called “21st century skills” are better thought of as Stone Age skills.

Trying to teach someone to speak or listen is a bit like trying to teach them to breathe. There are some useful tips — breathe through your nose, slow down when you’re anxious, don’t hold your breath when you’re lifting something heavy — but there aren’t many of them, and the returns diminish very quickly.

Confidence is easily mistaken for understanding, and someone has to decide what counts as good talk. A child who is extroverted and at ease with the conventions of middle-class speech will tend to do well whether or not they have anything worth saying.
If we start trying to assess all this we’ll be in danger of creating an invalid and unreliable means of measuring how middle-class kids sound.
